label: OLD:rep_att_a
name: Barge-Mounted Bluff Auger Coal
mech: Anchor: a spudded floating auger bores a frozen seam at water level in a river bluff and discharges straight into a hold, so no overburden is moved. At 20 kt/yr the rig sits idle most of the year and costs about 4,100 rub/t. The repaired version runs the whole ~100-day navigation season at about 60 t/h, for about 80 kt/yr. That rate sits between historical augers (21.5 t/h) and highwall miners (100–140 t/h). It fills four hopper barges moored alongside instead of its own hold. Thrust of 150–300 kN is taken by a frame bolted to the face, because three spuds (about 360 kN) are marginal. The frame has about 3 m of vertical travel to follow the 1–3 m drop in low-water stage during a campaign. Holes rise slightly so they drain. Face recovery is 62%, about 190 t per 80 m hole, which uses about 0.9 km of bluff a year.
value: About 1,800 rub/t at a village bank within 150 km. That compares with 2,800–3,700 rub/t for a pit at the bank under a 20–30 m bluff (1.6–2× cheaper) and 7,100–11,600 rub/t for coal hauled 2,000+ km, as from Dzhebariki-Khaya (4–6× cheaper). There is no gain under a bluff of 10 m or less.

label: OLD:rep_att_b
name: Ice-Deck Borehole Talik Mining
mech: Anchor: drill from winter lake ice into the sub-lake talik, which is already thawed, and mine the pay by borehole hydraulic mining. That means no thaw (saves 90 MJ/m³, about 25 kWh/m³), no dike, no drainage and no stripping. Repair: 1.2 m of ice carries only ~25 t of parked load, so the ice is flood-thickened to ≥1.8 m (Gold's formula at A=3.5 kg/cm² gives 113 t short-term, ~57 t parked). The 20-25 t modules sit more than 57 m apart, and the casing is insulated where it passes through the ice. Loose saturated talik gravel holds no roof and caves into the cavity, so the method is limited to narrow (25-40 m), deep, fine-gravel buried channels (<15 cm, the intake limit). Holes go on an 18 m grid (jet reach R=9 m) and are airlifted at 20-40 m³/h. Drawing stops at D≈3.4-3.9 m³ drawn per m³ of pay, set by on-ice jig grade monitoring; this extracts 86-89% of the pay in each hole's footprint, and tailings go back down mined holes. Cost: 1,130-1,970 rub per m³ drawn, which is 3,000-4,800 rub/g of gold recovered.
value: Recovers gold from narrow, deep sub-lake channels that today go unmined, at 3,000-4,800 rub/g. The cheapest alternative, a summer pontoon suction dredge, costs ≥8,800 rub/g, so this is 1.8-4.4x cheaper; on channels wider than 80 m it is only 1-1.5x cheaper.

label: OLD:rep_att_b
name: Channel-Talik Seam Dredging
mech: Anchor: a dredge cuts the coal seam in place inside the unfrozen channel talik, where the river has already removed the cover, and pumps it into a hopper barge. Repair: only seams at thalweg level under high bluffs, where a bank pit would have to strip 15-25 m³/t. A leased dredge with a 150 kW cutter cuts lignite (UCS 5-7 MPa) at 46-65 m³/h, which is about 46-65 t/h and matches Kovin's measured 67 t/h. A 10 kt village-cluster year therefore takes 8-25 dredge-days, not "a week", and one dredge visits about 4 bends a season. An on-barge dewatering screen brings the coal to ~32% moisture (3,670 kcal/kg). Cutting in June-July lets stockpiles drain before freeze-up. Delivered cost is 2,700-4,300 rub/t, which is 730-1,170 rub/Gcal.
value: 730-930 rub/Gcal with a shared dredge, against 2,830 rub/Gcal for northern-delivery coal at 15k rub/t (3.0-3.9x cheaper) and 1.4-2.4x below a bank micro-pit under high bluffs. There is no gain where the same seam has thin cover on land.

label: OLD:rep_att_b
name: Wintering Coal CHP Barge
mech: Anchor: the bunker barge that brings the winter's coal stays frozen in at the village and burns its own cargo as a combined heat and power plant. Repair: a thermal-oil coal boiler (80%) feeds an ORC (16% net), run heat-led into the village heat network. The 1.54 MW of reject heat replaces boiler-house coal burned at 65%, so the net extra fuel per kWh_e is about 0. Electric-only would cost 12.7 rub/kWh_e at 10k rub/t; the original 20-30x claim compared kWh of heat from coal with kWh of electricity from diesel. A 0.3 MWe unit needs 1,780 t of coal per winter, which fits one 2,000 t barge, and the 381 m³ of ash fits the hold space freed as coal is burned. Reject heat of 104 kW keeps an ice moat open around the hull and 44 kW keeps the hold unfrozen. Capex dominates the cost: 19-32 rub/kWh at 0.3 MWe (132-237 M rub) and 14 rub/kWh at 1 MWe for district centres.
value: Winter electricity at 14-32 rub/kWh against 45-75 rub/kWh full diesel cost (1.9-4.3x cheaper, up to 6x where costs reach 88 rub/kWh), with the heat nearly free.

label: OLD:compose_1
name: Frozen-bluff auger coal, shallow bunker hulls
mech: - A spudded floating auger (P5, repaired) bores a frozen coal seam in a 20-30 m river bluff during the 60-90 effective days of low water. The repairs use the reviewed 21-38 t/h at 75% availability and 30-50% field recovery, a frame with longer vertical travel, hole mouths kept above the campaign's low water, and remote operation from the tug with bluff monitoring. - It discharges straight into unpowered 2,000 t hulls drawing 1.26 m (P7). One tug and 3 hulls shuttle the coal 150-300 km to winter-road villages on a shoaling Yana/Indigirka-type river. This replaces about 2,000 km of river haul, a transshipment depot and about 450 km of winter road. - Coupling: low water is the only time the rig can reach the seam, and also the only time when nothing but hulls drawing 1.3 m or less can run the river (1,746-2,000 t payload at 1.5-2.0 m depth). The rig fills one hull every 5.9 days, so 3 hulls keep it loading with no mine stockpile, loader or transshipment. - Each hull's last cargo of the season winters loaded as the shore boiler-house's bunker, burned first (P7's anchor). The boiler stays on shore and the hull is empty by January. The coal leaves the seam frozen and has 8-26 days above 0 °C before air means fall below zero on about 21 Sep. Stokers cut a slot as the hull rises 0.96 m. No extra hull is needed. - Chains built with P4, P6 and the gold pieces all fell below 2x.
value: Fuel heat into village boilers costs 1,700 RUB/Gcal (1,360-2,160) against 4,380 today. That is 2.6x (2.0-3.2x; 20% chance of reaching 3x) against today's long-haul plus winter-road supply. Against the best competent alternative it is 0.82x (0.67-0.98): a bank pit at the same bluff with the same hulls is cheaper and on its own gives 3.2x. One rig supplies about 25 kt/yr, which is 12% of Arctic Yakutia's 205 kt of utility coal and about 8,300 people within 300 km of one bluff.

label: g1_ledger
name: Burnable timber rafts drift coal
mech: At a riverside pit such as Zyryanka, coal is loaded onto rafts made from local logs. About 2 m³ of logs carries 1 t of coal, assuming ~0.5 t of spare buoyancy per m³. The rafts are released on the spring flood and drift downstream (~100 km/day) to villages, which winch them ashore and burn both the coal and the logs. The closest earlier practice is the one-way Lena flatboats of the 17th–19th centuries (паузки), which were broken up at their destination; they lost out to steamers and diesel barges. Shoaling now caps those barges at under 50% load, while a raft draws only ~0.4 m and needs no fuel or return trip. The deciding quantity is the share of rafts lost or stranded over ~500 km, set against what logs cost at the pit.
value: Delivers the winter's fuel downstream for almost no transport cost, and the raft itself arrives as extra fuel.

label: g1_ledger
name: Frozen-in bunker-boiler barge
mech: A barge carries the full year's coal in summer and stays for the winter in a sheltered backwater (затон) next to the village. Its hold is the coal store, and a boiler module on deck feeds the village heat main through an insulated link to shore. Searches found no frozen-in boiler-barge case. The closest is Akademik Lomonosov, which at 70 MW was far too big for a village and overran its budget 4.1x. This design uses a standard river barge and an off-the-shelf boiler. The deciding quantity is hull survival through about 8 months of ice and the spring breakup flood, which existing backwater wintering of river fleets suggests is manageable.
value: Removes the winter-road last mile, the shore stockpile, double handling and a separate boilerhouse, which by these numbers roughly halves the cost of heat in the village.

label: g1_ledger
name: Downstream coal on empty barges
mech: On the Kolyma, the summer Northern Delivery convoys bring fuel and goods upstream from Chersky and come back down empty. They pass riverside pits like Zyryanka on the way, so they could carry coal down on that return leg. The cost is only marginal: a short loading stop plus a little extra draft. Return-cargo pricing is common in shipping, but no Kolyma coal-on-the-return contract was found. Such cargo normally fails when directions do not match, and here they do. The deciding quantity is how much load the empty barges can take at late-season water depths, given that shoaling already limits loaded barges to under 50%.
value: Cuts the barge cost per tonne several-fold using vessels that already make the trip, with no new capital.

label: g1_neg
name: Frozen-in barge boilerhouse
mech: A barge from the ageing Lena/Kolyma fleet, near scrap value, gets a containerised boiler and a 2–3 kt coal hold. It arrives at the settlement on high water and is frozen in at a berth, with an air-bubbler kept running to stop ice pressure. All winter it burns its own cargo and sends heat to shore through an insulated pipe. This deletes three steps: transshipment, the shore stockpile and the winter-road last mile. The closest attempt is the Akademik Lomonosov floating plant, which was stopped by 70 MW of scale and a 4x capital overrun. This uses a written-off hull and a boiler of about 1–5 MW. Deciding quantity: annualised hull plus boiler cost per hold-tonne against the last-mile and handling share it removes (about 11,000–15,000 rub/t, est.). That share needs sourcing.
value: A settlement could be fuelled with no winter road and no shore coal yard.

label: g1_neg
name: Flood-crest barge launch
mech: Coal goes from the pit in winter and is loaded onto barges wintering in a sheltered backwater near it. The barges wait out the ice drift and leave on the spring flood crest. That way they travel fully loaded, not under 50% as on summer shoal water. The closest attempt is the "early delivery" voyages, which hit drifting ice and lost the crest. Here the barges shelter during the drift, and the timing is computed from gauge forecasts. Deciding quantity: the days between the reach clearing of ice and water falling below loaded draft, compared with the transit time.
value: The cost per tonne of the main barge haul roughly halves.

label: g1_neg
name: Ship char, not coal
mech: A small retort at the pit turns coal into low-moisture char and burns the off-gas for its own heat and the pit's power. The settlement then receives more energy per tonne shipped. Char also self-heats in stockpiles less than raw low-rank coal. The closest attempt is Termokoks at Berezovsky, which suited a large market, not Arctic settlement flows. Deciding quantity: energy kept per tonne of char divided by energy per tonne of coal (about 1.2–1.4x for low-rank coal, near 1 for higher-rank coking coal such as Zyryanka's).
value: Every tonne-km of a fixed-capacity chain carries about a quarter more heat.

label: g1_mech
name: Frozen-in barge boilerhouse
mech: A barge carries a full winter's coal in its hold and a containerised boiler on deck. In autumn it is moored and allowed to freeze in at a riverside settlement, and an insulated heat main of about 200 m runs ashore. The boiler burns straight from the hold all winter, so there is no unloading, no shore stockpile, no loader fleet and no second handling; the barge returns empty after breakup to refill at the pit. Barges already winter frozen-in in river backwaters, and no search found a barge used as boilerhouse and bunker (ATTEMPT 23). The deciding quantity is the share of the ~23,000 rub/t spent after the barge haul (handling, stockpile losses, last mile); it must exceed ~65% to reach 3x.
value: Riverside settlements could get boiler coal for roughly the cost of the barge haul alone.

label: g1_mech
name: Burnable flood-season cargo rafts
mech: In winter, crews at an upstream pit build log rafts or plank flatboats and load bagged coal onto them. The spring flood floats them downstream for 3-5 weeks at about 1-2 m/s, roughly 100+ km/day, using water too shallow for barges later in the season (ATTEMPT 22). At the settlement the hull is broken up and burned as fuel with the coal, so there is no return trip and the current does the hauling. The closest attempt is the 19th-century Lena *karbas* (disposable downstream boats), abandoned when steam barges beat hand labour; here the hulls are built in the idle winter season and their wood becomes delivered fuel. The deciding quantity is the fraction of rafts that arrive intact past gravel bars and ice jams; it must exceed ~85%.
value: Settlements downstream of small pits on minor rivers could be supplied without barges or winter roads.

label: g1_mech
name: Long-season tracked sled trains
mech: One wide-tracked tractor tows 8-12 low-pressure freight sleds over snow and river ice. Ground pressure is low enough to start in October and run into May, about 150+ days against the truck winter road's 45-54 (ATTEMPT 1). One driver moves 150-250 t instead of 25 t per truck, and sleds left at the settlement serve as the coal stockpile. The closest attempts are the 1950s Alaskan cat trains, displaced by trucks and air, and Antarctic traverses, which are costed for fuel loads rather than bulk coal; neither was set against a 45-day road window. The deciding quantity is cost per tonne-km; it must fall below ~5 rub/t-km against the winter road's 20.
value: Inland settlements beyond barge reach could get a winter supply route about three times longer and several times cheaper per tonne.
